items.body: Photo by Vins Pedata. Courtesy the artist Sven Fritz is an artist from Germany, who has various ongoing projects that explore performance, experimental music, and sound art. We had the chance to converse over email about his latest work, Der Saal tobt, realized under the Ervin Omsk moniker, published by Orange Milk. The interview was edited collaboratively with the artist. David Murrieta Flores (ACL): Hi Sven, could you please talk a bit about the Ervin Omsk project for readers who are unfamiliar with it? Sven Fritz (EO): Hi David, sure. Ervin Omsk is a pseudonym I’ve been using to release experimental electronic music since 2020. The name doesn’t actually have any special meaning; it’s simply an anagram of my two first names. The project began in 2018 with a few musical collages that were strongly connected to the idea of exploring an abstract painting or sculpture in a particular room—in other words, a very spatial approach, in which I combined diverse sounds from a modular system, field recordings, voice, and so on. Fortunately, Orange Milk was willing to release these tracks on tape in 2020, with artwork by Keith Rankin. In 2023, a second album, titled Schmalster Point, was released on vinyl, with artwork by Brenna Murphy. Now the third album, Der Saal tobt, is being released on tape and CD, with artwork by Lukas Schmenger. Ervin Omsk is currently one of several projects I’m working on. However, it’s the only solo project, and therefore also the most intense one. All my other projects are collaborative—for example, most recently with the French musician Amédée de Murcia. Together, we released an album in March on the Italian label Søvn. There’s also the Hui project, which I’m doing together with Johannes Schebler (Baldruin). An album has just been released on Jollies, and another one was released on Nonlocal Research last year. I’m also part of the artist collective Trickster, where I collaborate with other artists to realize scenarios in the sense of a Gesamtkunstwerk. My role here often involves musical performances lasting several hours and spread out over multiple days. All of my projects fall within the realm of experimental electronic music, and Ervin Omsk really benefits from the many experiences I’ve had working with all these other musicians. This applies not only to production, but also to the concerts I play as Ervin Omsk. These performances, however, are more like interpretations or improvised versions of the tracks I release. ACL: As the liner notes describe it, Der Saal tobt is mimicry of an orchestral body. Usually, we would understand such a body as mechanically efficient and well-coordinated, tuned and built through practice. However, the album understands it differently, and the result is slightly opposite: it’s a body that seems “unpracticed”. How do you understand the relationships between these bodies’ organs? How do you understand the differences between the modern, “well-oiled” orchestra and the album’s version of it? EO: I recently went to a concert where a chamber ensemble performed a piece that really moved me. At the same time, I realized that I actually didn’t really know what was going on. I have no academic background in this field. For example, I lack knowledge of music history and theory, notation, instrumentology, the roles within an ensemble, and so on. So I can only form a vague idea of what is happening in this music. I sense its dissonance, complexity, and openness; at times, it almost feels improvised. At the same time, I associate orchestral music with something highbrow and inaccessible. And that would be, so to speak, a different perspective from the outside. I generally have a rather ambivalent relationship with high culture, because it often caters to unchanging expectations and cultivates a kind of institutional sophistication. And in this context, the terms “efficient” and “coordinated” become interesting: these are actually very performance-oriented categories, which I would spontaneously associate with economics and sport. What do they have to do with music? But yes, an orchestra also needs this high degree of functionality, because, for example, it follows an idea or an order in the form of a notation. The musicians ensure that everything runs smoothly because they have mastered their instruments. To put it bluntly, we could argue that a modern, well-oiled orchestra must function—which sounds almost a bit cold and predictable. In music or art, however, I am not interested in categories like “well rehearsed,” “efficient,” and “coordinated” at first. It is rather the state outside these functions that moves me. To me, the intuitive and the seemingly contradictory have always been special qualities. There is, for example, that brief moment when an orchestra or a small ensemble tunes up. It is an undefined jumble of sounds, a wonderful moment of uncertainty. I am fascinated by the orchestra pit and its sound. But I come from a different musical background, both technically and culturally. I only play guitar, I can sing, and I know some things about synths and computer music. So I can’t imitate the orchestra; I can only bring electronic instruments into play, which then, through practice, become their own form of an orchestral body. And the interactions between the organs aren’t without tension; they sometimes get in each other’s way, and they don’t always speak the same language. And that’s what makes their relationships so special to me. There’s no oil here—more like sand in the gears and friction, to stick with your analogy. ACL: What is the process that you follow in order to craft a track? How do you understand the connections between tracks, once they are finished? EO: I can hardly describe it, really. There is no linear or additive process: each track is the result of countless intuitive decisions, right down to the smallest moments. I’m obsessed with details. The computer of course offers infinite possibilities and an overwhelming freedom. But that also means I usually can’t remember how the individual tracks were made. But I’ll try to describe it using the last track on the album as an example—which was actually the first track I produced: Right at the beginning, I made some very simple and short recordings of an alto recorder that I had borrowed from a friend and musician. After sampling and processing these recordings, the flute’s physical qualities were still there—the airiness, the directness, the softness, the hiss, and so on—but I could tune it freely and also control its overtones and noise, among other things. In fact, it suddenly seemed more like a symbol for an entire group of woodwind instruments or like an instrument that wanted to be several at once. And yet it still had something artificial about it. This impression was reinforced by the way it was played. Arpeggiators, whose tempo and rate were modulated by LFOs; animated envelopes that made glissandos possible; and the layering of several abstract flutes at once, varying only in their playing and sound. Then combined and blended with noises and glitches that picked up on the flutes’ patterns and intonations, countered them, and made them seem alien. Then it got a bit crowded, maybe like rush hour at the main train station. So then it was a constant process of sorting, resampling, stretching, compressing, cutting, copying, pasting, deleting, and leaving pauses—until the track was finished. Something like that, very roughly. And as I said, there’s no single process that applies equally to all tracks. Other tracks have undergone several transformations. They were actually finished; then I completely rearranged them in the context of the entire album, because they didn’t feel right within the album’s dynamic, and the sequence of the tracks that unfolds over just 27 minutes. In addition, on this album I deliberately used certain sounds—such as the processed alto recorder— in several tracks, either obviously or just as a trace. And then, for me, all the pieces take place in the same space; they’re close and direct. Photo of Trickster setup by Sven Fritz. Courtesy the artist. ACL: What sort of gear do you use in this process? Thinking of gear less in terms of straightforward tools, and more socially in terms of extensions of your own thoughts and body, what does all this gear allow you to do? What does it inhibit you from doing? EO: I always try not to own too much gear. Even in production, I use only a few very specific and experimental tools so as not to unnecessarily expand the range of possibilities: a small modular system, MIDI controllers, Ableton Live, with digital samplers, sound generators, M4L devices, a few effects, and then a few flutes and microphones. I like the second part of your question. As a child, I played a home organ—two manuals, bass pedals. After that, I played electric guitar and sang for a long time, always in the context of bands. Vocals and guitar, in particular, are two very direct and physical instruments. It’s almost impossible to transfer that feeling to the world of synthesizers and computers, because playing them is less about gestures and more about fine motor skills involving the hands, fingers, eyes and ears: knobs, pads, trackpads, clicking, looking, listening and so on. But when it comes to abstract thinking about music, synthesizers and computers offer another advantage. They expand the scope of what I can imagine musically and put me in a constant state of learning and wonder. It’s sometimes like a rush. Surely also because I don’t understand everything. But in any case, it changes my own perception of sound, because these machines basically function like auditory microscopes. You can dive incredibly deep with your ears and your thoughts. ACL: Going back to the idea of orchestration, do you understand yourself as the orchestra’s director? Perhaps the orchestra itself, as an abstract embodiment? Perhaps the orchestra’s prompt-maker, to use contemporary code? In short – what is your own position within or without the orchestral body of the album? EO: A prompt-maker relies on clear codes or language as commands, right? That wouldn’t be immediate enough. And unfortunately, I don’t know much about the work of a conductor. But if I may set that aside for a moment, it might be something between a conductor and the orchestra itself. Here’s how I picture it: there’s a room full of objects, no musicians. So I rush through the ranks and set these objects into motion, sound, gestures, and relationships with one another. That would be very closely linked to experiences with live performances—both the role of the conductor and the abstract embodiment. Two examples: There’s this collective project called Trickster, which I’ve already mentioned: very irregularly, we realize a series of evenings as an image—no hierarchy, no stage, no beginning, no end, and thus no mood-setting service. In one of the those projects, I arranged 6–8 different speakers, several mixers, an electric guitar, a spontaneous choir of friends, several synthesizers, a percussionist, and two friends playing the French horn and the soprano recorder, spread throughout a room of about 100 square meters. Here, my role was more like that of a conductor who, over the course of about five hours, activated and collaged all of this using clear impulses and several loopers. Charging and discharging the space, playfully and improvisationally. Then recently I put together a live setup for some shows that had to fit into a backpack. A computer, two MIDI controllers, a small semi-modular synthesizer, and a microphone for vocals. Yet I prepared it in such a way that there were always five different instruments that I could play simultaneously. That was a bit demanding, but very direct, all on a small table—more as if I were many instruments, or, if you will, the orchestra itself. Turning knobs, playing pads, plugging in cables, tuning, singing, applying effects, controlling, not controlling. Photo by Matt Favero. Courtesy the artist. ACL: I’d like to return now to the question of mimicry – it’s an aesthetically loaded term, but it’s possible to contrast it with the idea that there is something organic to the body we are listening to in the album. If we understand the album’s body as more of an automaton, what are its possibilities/capacities/abilities when thinking about traditional musical categories of representation like “expression”? EO: Oh, that’s a really tough question, and I’m not sure I fully understand it. Mechanization could also be understood as a rigid and hierarchical process, but the automaton of the album feels alive to me. That would be more like a cyborg, right? But sure, let’s stick with the image of the automaton. I don’t think of it as a concrete thing with a particular physical form, but rather as an abstract machine, as algorithms and processes. In order to see what abilities it has in terms of traditional musical categories, I have to listen to it. So I’ll pretend for a moment that I didn’t build the automaton. At first, it sounds to me like a machine that seems to define its own form, processes, and movements, acrobatic and unpredictable, like a shapeshifter. It leads an inscrutable life of its own. The mistakes it makes are constantly incorporated into its search for form. A complex and delicate act. But only on the first, and perhaps the second, listening. Once you have become familiar with the complexity, the mechanisms, and the glitches, the form and nature of the automaton become clearer. Perhaps that is the moment when we can return to the “category of representation,” once we have understood the language of the automaton. Because “musical expression” may not be as organic, immediate, and human as we like to think. It is also part of a tradition and works through codes, conventions, expectations, and learned gestures—only seemingly self-evident. The automaton, of course, is only indirectly part of this tradition. In this logic, perhaps the ability of the automaton does not lie in “expressing” something in the classical sense, but in using, shifting, exaggerating, or also refusing these codes of expression. It maybe has the potential to transform many different sounds, instruments, gestures, figures, and experiments into a different but nevertheless familiar form of expression. And perhaps through its artificiality and distance it can make something audible that a human body would not do in this way. But the question really is very abstract. I hope I was able to give a somewhat meaningful answer here. Photo by Tobias Ullrich. Courtesy the artist. ACL: You did, thank you! Now, I’m interested in the meaning of the various track titles. There’s a playful overtone about things going wrong, failing in wholesome ways, or simply being the result of an essay in something (the “Memo Grisaille”, for instance, which alludes to the formative, practical painting made in shades of black or grey that emerged in the Renaissance). What links the process through which you made each track with the titles you chose for them? EO: Collecting titles or sentences is an independent process that I and other friends have been practicing since art school. I’m interested in titles because they add an associative layer to the individual track or the entire album. The album artwork by Lukas Schmenger does that too, by the way. Like the artwork, the titles are an important part of the album, even though they only come into the process at a later stage. I think the titles of the album relate in a certain way to its dynamics and moods. So I really associate the album title “Der Saal tobt” with an image of an agitated and unrestrained group of people. A feeling and sound somewhere between threat and excitement maybe. At the same time, it’s important for me to break up some kind of sonic overload with an everyday and blunt remark like “Beim besten Willen,” which rather expresses a refusal or incomprehension. So I also like the laconic quality of titles. With “Memo Grisaille,” though, it wasn’t my intention to trivialize this art-historical term. I simply like the combination of the words in terms of their sound, and the piece has something fragile and searching about it, like a memory that only becomes sharp and distinct in certain moments. So, with each title, there is an association that relates to the mood of the piece—with it or against it. ACL: Your previous album already explored a sense of joy derived from electronic sound interactions. Considering the track title themes, I think the argument can be made that there’s a humorous undercurrent in Der Saal tobt – there’s a philosophical perspective that says, basically, that it’s funny when things act like persons, but also the other way around. As the album’s automaton furiously fumbles around, we could be inspired to laugh: have you ever thought of experimental electronic music as possibly funny? Would you see a role for humor within your work, in the past, now, and in the future? EO: Experimental electronic music can be fun, sure. But so far, I haven’t gotten that feeling from this album. Then again, maybe I’m just missing something because I wasn’t sitting at the instruments or in front of the computer laughing while making it. Maybe it’s already fun when something unexpected happens. The staging of errors that make the automaton seem human, the unusual sounds, the friction in the gears, getting tangled up in the gestures—all of that could be interpreted as fun. For me, these are necessities, because I fear a well-oiled machine—and thus the predictable. And perhaps also I can’t take things, or myself, too seriously. So there may, after all, be a certain humorous distance, and therefore an unconscious influence on the tracks. But as the author myself, I can’t hear it. And that means humor would not have a defined role right now. If anything, it just happens, as it does in encounters with other people. For me, humor is indispensable there. In any case, I want to keep thinking about your question. There are quite a few inspiring examples in music, but also in visual art, that I would definitely describe as humorous. And maybe humor can get a more definite role in my work too. ACL: Thank you very much for your time, Sven. Is there anything else you’d like to tell our readers before closing this interview? EO: I’d like to thank you for these really challenging and intense questions. They went quite deep, and I found it very inspiring to think about them. Now I’m curious to know what it’s like to listen to the album after reading this interview—how it affects the way we perceive and contextualize this music. Especially since the album doesn’t necessarily need a strong conceptual framework, as it was created largely intuitively. Talking about it this way now almost feels like a kind of mental post-production, even though the music is already finished. And I consider it something special in itself to be able to release music like this, in the hope that there will be a few people out there who will actually listen to it and perhaps even find something in it. Thanks again for this opportunity.

items._cn_summary: 德国艺术家Sven Fritz以Ervin Omsk为名发行的第三张专辑《Der Saal tobt》，通过模块化合成器、现场录音与人声等多元素材构建出空间化的声音拼贴。专辑概念围绕对'管弦乐团体'的模拟展开，但呈现的并非训练有素、精密协调的集体，而是一种去技能化的、混乱的声响群像。这种'未排练的合奏'打破了传统乐队的协调逻辑，将不同声源置于相互碰撞的拓扑关系中，让各自的纹理与故障自然浮现。作品延续了Ervin Omsk自2018年以来的探索脉络，从抽象绘画与雕塑的空间感出发，质疑了集体演奏中身体与器官的隐喻关系。

items.body: Power up the hi-fi and get your favorite seventies era Sci-Fi laserdisc movie cued up on your vintage home entertainment system, turn the volume down on the film, and turn up the volume on OBA to let them provide the soundtrack. An instant soundtrack to your inner movie, or your outer one OBA by OBA   Power up the hi-fi and get your favorite seventies era Sci-Fi laserdisc movie cued up on your vintage home entertainment system, turn the volume down on the film, and turn up the volume on OBA to let them provide the soundtrack. Turning the TV down and the stereo up is something old headz used to do. Out pattern making tendencies will find parallels with the visuals on the tube and the sounds from the music matching up in eerie ways. Look how far this took the acid addled minds of people who did this with the Wizard of Oz and the Dark Side of the Moon! OBA has provided an instant soundtrack to your inner movie, or your outer one. The project got started when three friends from three different continents found themselves in the same place and made a recording session, as musical friends are wont to do. The frequency wizard Amir Khay Nir from the USA, had met up with Orri Dror from Iceland, and Benjamin Esterlis in Israel. All of these fellows are multi-instrumentalists, making this an outing in overdubs after the initial recordings. But it is so freaking solid you think it was all happening live, and that’s the beauty of the recorded medium. It can make a live band out of a trio who live in far flung corners of the world. When I hear this music, I can see them playing, even it was completed after the initial sessions, and even if I don’t know what any of them look like. Synth’s swoon around drums, guitar and bass from the opening tones in an energetic weave. Not long after opening on “Ptaltalim” it starts to sound like a blurred VHS tape with bad tracking, but just for a second. The edited imperfection makes you awake to the perfection of the music, all moving into an action packed, almost aggressive soundscape of tight knit interlinking rhythms. What stands out: Intertwined souls: The chords and melodies played here make you know that you are listening to a group of people who are at ease musically syncing to each other despite the normal distances that separate them on the globe. We hear how the bass and guitar dialogues in pleasure with percolating synth, and whispers of flute as they paint the air and space and space with sound in a mood of sonic freedom. Emotional narrative: Though there is no voice and there are no lyrics in this entirely instrumental album, it moves naturally along an arc of action, reverie, intimation, and release across seven songs. It’s a soundtrack, but you make up the movie in your head. Chromatic resonance: From the melancholic power of “Luna Gal” to the electro-baroque impressionism of “Ketem” and progressive passages reminiscent of long time favorites such as Klaus Schulze, the album progresses like a well-structured musical short story (it’s a short and concise album) even as it permutates along the lines of something out of the studio of Gottfried Michael Koenig. Calculated chaos: All the notes are in the right place, and though there are a lot of notes, it’s not about showing off virtuosity. The skill of the players is in service to each composition. It’s a sincere work paying homage to classic forms, showing those forms are just as exciting when made anew. A touch of acid: Psychedelic inspiration is prominent throughout this work which invites dark room, eyes closed, introspective listening for out of body time. New listens reveal new textures, emotion and the craftsmanship that goes with attention to detail. OBA is available on Schwarz Neon Licht. [Bandcamp] OBA by OBA  The post OBA :: OBA (Schwarz Neon Licht) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.

items._cn_summary: OBA由来自美国、冰岛、以色列三位跨洲际音乐人远程合作完成，以多乐器叠加录音方式构建出浑然一体的器乐作品。专辑被乐评形容为七十年代科幻电影的即兴配乐，合成器与鼓、吉他、贝斯交织缠绕，闪烁出迷幻光泽。低保真噪点与磁带失真被刻意保留，反而强化了音乐的有机质感。七首曲目沿动作—冥想—暗示—释放的情绪弧线展开，无人声无歌词，却拥有完整的叙事张力。从《Luna Gal》的忧郁力量到《Ketem》的电声巴洛克印象主义，再到对Klaus Schulze式渐进展开的致敬，专辑在频谱调色上展现出沉稳的实验意识，既是三人默契的远程共振，也是声音在空间中自由穿梭的证明。

items.body: Melodic gestures emerge from drone surrounds—ground to figure, dissolving into field—drawing you in from perception’s margins, receding just as they seem to have settled. A platform to explore themes of presence, absence, removal and acceptance Disappear in Silent Ways by Halftribe   At the intersection of ambient, drone and environmental sound you’ll find Halftribe. His return to Dronarivm, Disappear in Silent Ways, comes in colors at once luminous and blurred, with a captivating ambi[val]ence, evoking a sense of moments presenting with past inside. Evanescence. This is achieved partly via a keen melodic sensibility with soft analog-y synths, field captures and odd voice fragments crafted into tone poems at once expansive and intimate. A form of minimalism runs through DiSW, manifest not in ideological stance but simple compositional practice; Ryan Bissett eschews the impulse for new entries to the sound stage for letting sounds evolve, adding color to broader canvas before letting in other elements. Sounds recede then return, revenant—a vague sense of movement over overt development; a soft ebb-flow dynamic, harmonic shifts emerging to color tenor, drones privileging depth over density, minute tonal shifts reframing space around and within. Melodic gestures emerge from drone surrounds—ground to figure, dissolving into field—drawing you in from perception’s margins, receding just as they seem to have settled. A site of refuge found after disappearing :: “Listen,” bids us attend to our environs, with its leitmotif ‘what we listen to is constantly feeding us’ adjuring mindfulness of what we let in. Field recordings bring in the natural world, as on “Dusk,” mixing layered drones with rainfall, evoking crepuscular horizons in day-night transition, inner-outer boundaries dissolved; or “Sanctuary,” pointing to a site of refuge found after disappearing; its oneiric mood feeds into “Yearn,” water flow enhancing a sense of peace through nature connection. “Windfall” shifts focus from water, distant whispers suggesting a field with grass and trees windblown, light filtering through branches to slow cloud drift. The title track brings an interlude of release, with birdsong and babbling before “Everything Comes to an End” leaves us with… that sense of evanescence. Following For the Summer, or Forever (2018) and Elegant, Golden (2022), Dronarivm has provided Halftribe with a platform to explore themes of presence, absence, removal and acceptance. The artist’s stamp, though, is more outline than full imprint, DiSW not looking to thematic statement so much as documenting the resonance of a feeling, in all its contours. Disappear in Silent Ways is available on Dronarivm [Bandcamp] Disappear in Silent Ways by HalftribeThe post Halftribe :: Disappear in Silent Ways (Dronarivm) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.

items._cn_summary: Halftribe 新作《Disappear in Silent Ways》由 Dronarivm 厂牌发行，横跨环境音乐、持续音与环境声三大领域。创作者 Ryan Bissett 以柔和的模拟合成器音色、田野录音与碎片化人声构建出一种兼具广阔感与私密感的音诗，旋律线条从持续音背景中浮现又消融，如同感知边缘的微弱信号。专辑贯彻一种实践层面的简约主义——拒绝不断叠加新声部，而是让声音自然演化、通过细微的音调变化重塑空间感。曲目编排上，《Dusk》混合降雨声与多层持续音营造黄昏渐暗的氛围，《Sanctuary》与《Yearn》以水流声呈现梦境般的庇护所意象，《Windfall》则借助远处低语暗示风吹草地的田野场景。终曲以鸟鸣与潺潺水声收束，留下一抹消散之感。整体而言，这张专辑以旋律敏感性与声学质感记录了关于在场、缺席、放下与接纳的情感共振，而非追求明确的主题宣言。

items.body: Parissior is a Spanish project founded by DJ and producer Jesu Aparicio. With “Human Control”, he releases his debut album, featuring ten tracks (although the vinyl edition contains only eight). While several EPs were released previously, this album consists entirely of new material, exploring themes such as digital identity, illusion, authenticity, and human imperfection. Musically, this translates into a very solid mix of Dark-Techno and EBM. The basslines sound menacing and pure EBM, while the kicks reveal clear Techno influences. There are also a few additional influences, such as Acid sequences, as well as some delightful old-school Techno elements that remind me of the Frankfurt scene of the 1990s. The way everything is put together sounds intelligent and, naturally, highly dancefloor-oriented. There are also some vocals worth mentioning, including a track featuring guest vocalist Jorge Tornin, although the vocals are not necessarily the most striking aspect of the album. “Human Control” is a very strong release that delivers a perfect blend of nostalgic moments and a more contemporary sound, in which Dark-Techno and EBM are inseparable and form a powerful cocktail. An album you absolutely must discover! (Rating:8½). Listen to “Eco Machines”: Eco Machines by Parissior About Parissior Parissior is the alias of Spanish DJ and producer Jesu Aparicio. He has released singles and EPs since at least 2016, including “Could I Drown In Your Desire” and “Dance To The Groove” (Spa In Disco), followed by “Let Them Dance” (Hot Digits Music, 2017) and further EPs and compilation appearances for Golden Soul Records. From “Back To Earth” (2020) onward he has worked mainly with the Espacio Cielo label, releasing further singles, EPs and compilation tracks including “Battle Cry” (2021), “Raver In The Booth” and “Full of Stars” (2023), and the Skylax release “Antennae” (2024). “Human Control” is his first full-length album.

items._cn_summary: 西班牙制作人Jesu Aparicio以Parissior之名发行的首张全长专辑，围绕数字身份、幻象与人类不完美等主题展开创作。整体呈现Dark-Techno与EBM的紧密交织：贝斯线凶狠纯粹，底鼓显露清晰的Techno血脉，Acid序列与九十年代法兰克福场景的怀旧质感穿插其中，结构编排兼具智识感与舞池功能性。部分曲目加入人声客串，但器乐与节奏设计才是核心。专辑在怀旧情绪与当代制作之间取得平衡，融合自然流畅，既向电子舞曲传统致敬，也展现出独立的制作视角。作为独立厂牌作品，兼具地下气质与可听性，是一张融合了类型历史与个人表达的扎实首作。

items.body:
There is a substantial list of attributes that sets Ran Blake apart from every other innovative pianist of the past sixty-plus years, each of which falls under one of two headings: his choice of materials and his treatments of them. The former is based on Blake’s ability to hear connections between materials for which “disparate” is an inadequate descriptor. Who else would sequence Max Roach’s “Mendacity” and “Saving All My Love for You” – or “On Top of Old Smokey” and Michel Legrand’s “Watch What Happens”? Nobody, because what Blake does is unique. He doesn’t interpret materials as much as administer an MRI, revealing the connective tissues and vital organs as vividly, if not more so, than the skeletal structure. In the process, Blake makes the familiar sound radically new.

Blake’s collaborations with singers are central to his work. The current critical consensus is that his groundbreaking work with Jeanne Lee overshadows everything since, the respective qualities of notables like Christine Correa and Sara Serpa notwithstanding. Roots & Byways circumvents the edifice The Newest Sound Around has become, primarily because Dominique Eade takes a different tact. She is not as rooted as Correa – or Lee, for that matter – in Billie Holiday, and she is not as committed to understatement as Serpa. Like both Correa and Serpa, Eade can shape a song syllable by syllable and render a highly personal interpretation. It is Eade’s palpably deep joy in singing that sets her apart, one that is not only bursting at the seams on showstoppers like the Whitney Houston megahit, but one that even seeps into noirish songs like Mingus’ “Portrait.” It is the key to her relatability and appeal, and to that of the album, as well.

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑的核心在于钢琴家Ran Blake对素材的独特处理方式——他将看似毫无关联的作品并置，如Max Roach与流行金曲、Mingus与民谣，在这种对比中以类似医学影像扫描的方式揭示音乐之间的深层连接与内在结构，使熟悉旋律焕发全新的面貌。Eade的演唱同样关键：她既不像Jeanne Lee那样扎根于Billie Holiday的语感，也不追求Christine Correa的克制或Sara Serpa的内敛，而是以逐字逐句雕琢歌曲的方式注入一种明显的喜悦感。这种情绪在Whitney Houston的热门金曲中尤为奔放，即便在Mingus的阴郁作品里也渗透出来。专辑绕开了此前被奉为标杆的声乐爵士框架，建立在钢琴独奏与歌手合作的基础上展开再诠释，为听众提供了一种介于传统与实验之间的聆听路径。

items.body: "There is no such thing as a stranger�s children." - old Ukrainian saying I�ve long been affected, indeed somewhat obsessed, by what�s happening in Ukraine, partly because of one of my favorite bands, DakhaBrakha. I went to Kyiv to see them at the time of the Maidan protests, just after the shooting by snipers of over a hundred protesters. I intentionally didn�t read this album�s booklet notes before listening, so that I could react to it without sympathetic pre-judgement, just as music. It�s strong musically and vocally by any standards, Ukrainian or otherwise. When I did then turn to the notes that translate and explain the songs, I had that rare experience, for me, of becoming moist-eyed. The songs are a mix of traditional and original. They are focused on the abduction by Russia of about 20,000 Ukrainian children who have been taken from their parents in Russian-occupied eastern Ukraine and sent to Russia, in an attempt to turn them into haters of their native land and people. It�s a heinous war crime. Marichka is a Ukrainian-Canadian singer who moves between Canada and her homeland. For this album she�s gathered two groups of musicians, one in each country. Both ensembles contribute vocals and instrumentation, mostly bowed strings, plus some bandura and piano. The group in Ukraine includes Lisa from the destroyed and invaded city of Mariupol, playing a solo on double ocarina; at 16 she was one of the stolen children but managed to return to Ukraine. Daughters of Donbas � co-led by Marichka and singer/bandurist Alina Kuzma, who shares the lead vocal role � is an all-female ensemble in Canada that tours performing these songs. �Foreign Land� is a reworking of a traditional song about the young girls who were sent away to work in foreign households - Marichka�s grandmother was one of these - that can also be taken to refer to the plight of today�s stolen children. The translation goes: A mother packed up her daughter To leave for a strange land To a strange land with strange people Oh, who will pity you, my daughter? Those who will beat me will pity me I'll never again live with you, my mother When, my daughter, should I expect you to come home? When the grass in the garden grows, my mother The grass grew and grew and began to dry The mother was waiting for her daughter to return, and began to cry Did you hear, my mother, how I came to you? How I flew as a bird above your window? How I cooed like a dove? If, my daughter, I could hear you I would open all the doors and windows To let you fly in Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Alina Kuzma, Zo� Santo As befits the song, Marichka�s vocal here is gentle. But in the second track, �Rusalka,� with Alina Kuzma taking the lead vocals, things turn harsh and fierce. A rusalka is a mythical creature, a nature spirit of fields, forest and rivers, that features in traditional ritual songs. The melody of this one is by Zo� Santo and Kuzma, with lyrics drawing on tradition and the composition of Santo and 19thC Ukrainian poet and folklorist Taras Shevchenko. An ominous double-bass drone, chunking strings, a slithering vocal that moves into sections of white-voice fast recitative and expands into a soaring wild cry. The lyrics are very dark, perhaps evoking the hell of the front line: Home a hell of old growth stumps Marsh a mud of memories Don�t get bogged down in these parts Your kind won�t last a day in here While witches still fly, while roosters have yet to crow, Come here, something arises, �neath the oak something walks. A rusalka sat on a white birch, rusalky asked girls for shirts. Long fingers and nails so sharp Tongue forked round serrated teeth Moss grows down beneath her parts Weeds braided from ear to ear While witches still fly, while roosters have yet to crow, Come here, something arises, �neath the oak something walks. �Girls, my friends, give me your shirts. Though I�m thin, give me a thin one.� Here live us the backless ones Many voices of dead sons You are right to quake in fear Send your sinful children here �Who Am I� is a plea of separation and disorientation, the pain and confusion of an abducted child, contrasting �the human in me� and �the creature in me,� like an internalized riddle-song, with the refrain, in English: Who am I for you? Who am I for me? Do you know me? Really know me? �Enchantress,� passionately sung by Kuzma to her own bandura accompaniment, a girl�s lament of the loss of her brave love taken from her by the enchantress, who is an allegory of war, is based on a traditional song and uses that style of melody and lyrics, �Riddle,� sung by Marichka, reworks a traditional riddle song to be the riddles told by the grandfather of a child, 12-year-old Kira from Mariupol, who experienced the death of her father and her abduction to Russia. Her grandfather tracked her down, and brought her back, traumatized, and asked her riddles - as the notes say �to jog her memory, and remind her who she was, where her home was, and of her family�s love for her.� Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Marichka �4.5.0� is a military expression for �all�s well� or �all is quiet.� The song is a message, as from a mother, to a stolen child. Marichka�s voice is cherishing: Remember this: I am with you, I am here Don't give up, I'm with you. Don't give up, I'm with you Your hope is my weapon Don't be sad, I'm with you 4.5.0. will be again �breaking into a tearing howl: And when the world's axis breaks When the sky folds like a parchment Out of nowhere her words will come� �and back to fragile reassurance �It's all right, I'm here, I'm here� "Lullaby," based on a traditional lullaby, sung by Alina Kuzma to accompaniment by her bandura and Zo� Santo's viola, starts in gentle lullaby style, but moves to a lament; it's for the stolen children and those who, as the notes put it, 'have been stolen for ever.' Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Marichka �Remember, I Believe in You� is a powerful piece of harmonizing vocals and slithering strings. Here�s the story it�s based on: Yevhen lived in Mariupol with his three young children. During the siege they lived in a basement bomb shelter for months. One day, Russian soldiers entered their bomb shelter. Yevhen was taken to a filtration camp and separated from his children who were all taken to a hospital and then to Russian summer �camp�. In the filtration camp Yevhen was brutally tortured and forced to sleep standing on one leg. He tried to fall asleep, whispering prayers for his children: �Everything will be fine, I believe in you.� After his release he walked 30 kilometers to the place where his children had been taken but it was too late. They had already been sent to Moscow. Yevhen learned of this after receiving a text from one of his children who had found an unattended device. He traveled thousands of kilometers, crossed the borders of three countries, endured checks, interrogations and danger to reach Moscow and take his children home. All those days he tirelessly repeated to himself, �I believe in myself, I believe in my kids. Everything will be good.� �Another Heaven,� sung by Marichka with the ensemble in Ukraine, is inspired by another heart-rending story: Ilya was 9 years old when his mother was killed by a rocket strike right in front of him. He was taken to a hospital in occupied Donetsk, where 15 pieces of shrapnel were removed from his body without anesthesia. After he appeared in a report on Russian television, Ilya�s grandmother learned his location. She managed to bring her grandson to Kyiv, where he lives now, experiencing missile attacks every night. At age 11, he says that it is up to everyone to fight enemies, to protect other cities, and to build another heaven, where your home will not be destroyed. In 2014, during the Kyiv Maidan protests, Marichka wrote and performed �Red Boots Tango,� using a melody she�d put to a poem by Taras Shevchenko. For this album she sings it again in Ukraine, with the ensemble there adding swirling, classic tango-style strings. Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, BanduraGirl The final track on the album is a solo, recorded in Kyiv, by Anastasiya Voytyuk, accompanying herself on the older, simpler form of bandura that was used by kobzars to accompany epic poetry, and also on the nowadays more well-known big, heavy form developed from it in Soviet times that was made mainly in the piano factory at Chernihiv. Her song, �Soon I Will Be Back,� is based on a poem by novelist, journalist and war crime researcher Victoria Amelia, who was killed in 2023, in the city of Kramatorsk in Donbas, by a Russian rocket. Find the artist online. Further reading: Otava Yo - Do You Love (Review) Sofia Rei - Umbral (Review)

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑围绕乌克兰战争中约两万儿童被俄罗斯强制带离家园的真实事件展开，将传统民歌与新作融为一体，弓弦乐器、班杜拉琴与钢琴交织构建出深沉的情感底色。演唱者Marichka兼具乌克兰与加拿大背景，召集两支音乐团体分别在两国录制，玛里乌波尔幸存少女Lisa以双陶笛吹奏的独奏段落尤为动人。歌词取材自传统'异乡'主题，讲述被送往远方做工的少女，与当下被掳走的儿童命运形成跨时空呼应。乐评人强调专辑在不了解背景的情况下首先作为音乐打动了自己，随后才因歌词含义动容，说明作品在纯音乐层面也具备独立的感染力。作为源自东欧的非主流音乐地带作品，承载了沉重的历史叙事与文化记忆。

items.body: For an overview of the what, the why, and the where of this music, do read my review of Volume 1 of this series. Essentially, this collection is more of what made Volume 1 so infectious. Yet, what makes this music so fascinating in general, that is, beyond its unswerving ability to fill dance floors, is the fact that these two islands, part of the Paises Africanos de Lingua Oficial Portuguesa (PALOP) regions of the world, are the second smallest African country; Seychelles is smaller. There are only 12 villages on Sao Tom�, lots of rain forest and, not surprisingly, lots of rain. I mention this because one could be fooled into thinking, with music like what�s on offer here, there must have been a music scene larger than there actually was. Not that little was happening, but that less got recorded or released than it might have had there been a city such as Lagos or Nairobi with the studios, labels, and pressing plants to better document it all. The music here, like Volume 1- recorded during Africa�s so-called golden age- is known as Puxa, a complex stew of ingredients from other former African Portuguese colonies mixed with rhythms that, with the help of dancers, can summon spirits or exorcise demons. At least according to some. It�s worth knowing that a 100 years or so ago, the Portuguese banned Puxa dance; it�s also worth knowing they appear to have failed miserably at this silly endeavor. Tucked away in modern Puxa is merengue, Kompas, Soukouss, Benga, and much else. One suspects much of this is coincidental, while other grooves were definitely imported considering both Portuguese rule and the islands� location over the Atlantic from the Caribbean. But don�t be fooled into thinking these two islands don�t have their own thing, as the sounds on this collection show. L�VE L�VE Vol. 2: Sao Tom� & Principe Sounds 70s-80s - Pedro Lima Pedro Lima, who has featured in his own Bongo Joe collection, leads a fiery band, complete with choked guitar vamps tussling with a kit drummer as a lead guitar comments from the sidelines on �Sossegado.� Elsewhere, Sangazuza demonstrates what happens when the bass and keys drop out, leaving the drummers and guitars to ride out a groove and drive dancers mad in the process. Check �Sono s� ku� de t�ma� or �Mairo bi cedo� for their ability to place a firm finger on the pulse. Over 15 tracks, the collection shows off multiple guitars weaving and circling one another, with lead and harmony vocals constantly in response, becoming part of the songs� melodic framework. At any given moment, vocals give way as the music unspools and floats on grooves that must have gone on for hours live. Africa Negra�s �Apoi�mos a luta dos nossos irm�os� is one example. L�VE L�VE Vol. 2: Sao Tom� & Principe Sounds 70s-80s by Various Artists In general, what�s on offer here, like Volume 1, was recorded at Radio Sao Tom� e Principe (RSTP), often taped in the courtyard outside at night, and released on cassette or occasionally, vinyl. It captures the joy of post-1975 independence and only fizzled out as styles changed and musicians struggled to make ends meet. Yet, take a quick listen to recent RSTP programming, which features musicians such as Babilonia or Calema, and you�ll still hear Puxa rhythms, showing just how potent the music form this two-island nation is on a global level. And Bongo Joe, who have also released two volumes featuring the above mentioned Africa Negra, have given this music the treatment it deserves, with extensive notes on the country�s history, vintage photographs, and band discographies. items.body: A confession to begin: I�ve been a fan of Alison Cotton�s music for quite a while, so the announcement of a new album definitely brought me a frisson of delight. The Gods Laugh certainly doesn�t disappoint, with the same deliciously amorphous feel that�s defined her other work, drawing on folk, the avant-garde, as well as a sense of religiosity to make the music here, possibly best exemplified in �I Am!�, where she set a poem by John Clare, England�s great nature poet, to a transcendent melody over the constant underpinning of a lulling drone. While the playing revolves around her usual arsenal of viola, harmonium, hammered dulcimer, and piano, along with some percussion, on this album she also adds some drums, bass and synthesizer. The music is often improvised and captured in a single take, with an almost mystical, hushed sensibility that seems to reach through time, as with �I Still Know You are Calling My Name,� where the tune could have been plucked from an old folk song. Sprigs of Heather by Alison Cotton The centerpiece, however, is �Sprigs of Heather,� with an opening that recalls medieval sacred music that becomes a simple, slowly cascading, piano-led melody. It�s far from the longest track on the album, but a little pearl of perfection that carries the listener away. Sprigs of Heather by Alison Cotton The Gods Laugh is a memorial of sorts to Cotton�s father, who died in late 2024. There�s a sense of loss reaching across these tracks, most specifically present on �The Final Harvest,� a solemn piece about her father�s last visit to the allotment he loved so much. It�s suffused with tenderness that extends beyond words. Light and darkness bleed into each other across the music, and moods shift. It�s music that happily stands beyond category, with hints of so many things, but ultimately standing as Alison Cotton music, which might well be all the definition it needs. It will challenge you but also satisfy and move you. What more can you wish from music? Find the artist online. items.body: Tako Toki are like desert island musicians who, castaway without their instruments, were forced to construct their own. Lucky for us, they are as skilled in making instruments as they are in creating original songs with which to show off their handicrafts. Un Dimanche � Monaco is the band�s follow-up to their well-received debut, Hirsute Farfelus , with a similar mash of musical styles. Before discussing the music, we need to talk about their instrument closet. They really have built everything they play out of bric-a-brac, odds and ends, and rubbish. I�m not sure from listening which is which, but they call their instruments, in an incomplete list, tassofons, tilofons, and tubofones, clarinuts, didjerimou, and klarbass, and my favorite, kitchenofon. (I will refer to what I hear by the names of store-bought instruments that they sound like.) The most surprising thing for me was how accurate the instruments were to pitch and how good they sounded under the harsh scrutiny of modern recording microphones that have documented a rich, high-quality sound. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki They have also very effectively matched their choice of instruments with the style of music that inspires their compositions. Right off the top, �Yinitza� features a laughing clarinet singing a klezmer tune accompanied by bassoon for the bass, frantic two-time percussion, and the exuberant human yelps found on many klezmer recordings. As on this track, many tunes feature improvisations that show an impressive degree of musicianship. On the cumbia-inspired �Le Cuenta,� the characteristic flute carries the tune, augmented by a Spanish singing chorus, and remarkably rich-sounding Latin percussion. The title track surrounds us with afrobeat woodblocks, shakers, and rattles scattered around the mix. The melody is played on a marimba ornamented with bells and cymbals. Again, the lead player improvises over the tune and often against the beat with jazzy chops. The flute returns on the samba-inspired �Ambiguidade,� and on �Aksum� it traces a trance-like Middle Eastern tune reminiscent of a 60s TV spy-show theme. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki Full of fun and one of a kind, Un Dimanche � Monaco celebrates our universal love of rhythmic, melodic, and harmonic sounds and the varied, wonderful ways cultures have organized that love in what we call music. At the same time, playing on literal pieces of junk, Tako Tiko reminds us, as we contemplate many mall music shops filled with gleaming wood and brass instruments and countless unused guitars lying in closets, that musicians will always find a way to make music. Find the artist online. Further reading: Tako Toki - Hirsute Farfelus (Review) Terje Isungset - Glacial Poetry (Review)

items._cn_summary: Tako Toki 这支乐队的成员亲手用废旧物品自制乐器，包括名为 tassofons、kitchenofon 的奇异装置，却能在现代录音条件下保持精确音高与丰富音色。其第二张专辑将克莱兹默、昆比亚、非洲节拍、桑巴、中东旋律等多种世界音乐风格混融一体，乐器选择与音乐风格高度契合。克莱兹默曲调由自制单簧管引领，配以巴松与急促节奏；昆比亚风格曲目则交由长笛主奏，叠加西班牙语合唱与层次丰富的拉丁打击乐。专辑展现出乐队成员扎实的器乐演奏能力与即兴功底，每首曲目都呈现不同文化语境下的节奏与旋律逻辑。整体气质介于手工艺、世界音乐融合与即兴演奏之间，是对跨文化音乐语言的一次轻松而富实验性的探索。

After the extra-terrestial explorations of
Eventyrferd
, the previous album from Norway's Camilla Hole Trio, in which sci-fi synth sounds were married with traditional material, their latest release

items.body: After the extra-terrestial explorations of Eventyrferd , the previous album from Norway's Camilla Hole Trio, in which sci-fi synth sounds were married with traditional material, their latest release Langs is rather more earthbound. But the quest to look beyond their own country's folk music continues. Camilla Hole's main instrument being the soprano sax, the influence of jazz is unsurprising and this is evident in the opening track �Springleik,� signifying a tune used to accompany the springleik dance from the west of Norway. Initially Hole takes the melody with Egil Kalman and Knut Kvifte Nesheim providing rhythmic support on double bass and drums respectively, with the overdubbing of Kalman's modular synth and Nesheim's vibraphone adding colour. But characteristically for this trio, in which assigned roles are never clearly defined or adhered to, things soon start to move around, with Kalman taking up the melody on his bass, playing the melody in unison with Hole, while Nesheim opens things out further rhythmically. As the whole piece takes on a much more improvisatory feel, Hole plays the melody one more time as things draw to a close. Langs by Camilla Hole Trio

items.body: Kr�ta , the latest release on Norway's Taragot label, features a Swede and two Norwegians playing interpretations of mainly traditional tunes from their respective countries. Fiddler Mats Ed�n has long been involved in Swedish folk music, as a player, composer and teacher, and in the process exploring and integrating different musical styles and approaches. Tellef Kvifte was in the pioneering Norwegian crossover band Slinkombas in the 1970s and has continued to play a central role in Norwegian folk music, both as a musician and an academic. Most often heard playing the sj�fl�yte , more widely known as a recorder, Kvifte has employed other instruments from outside the Norwegian tradition, in particular the saxophone and bagpipes. His son Knut Kvifte Nesheim , a drummer and composer, has also shown a determination to blur the lines between different musical genres, both in his solo and group projects. Kr�ta by Ed�n/Kvifte/Nesheim trio It comes as no surprise then to find this trio offering a far from conventional take on the tunes they have chosen. While dance tunes may be the source of most of the material here, this feels more akin to chamber music; not that it is remotely classical in style, but in the sense it conveys of three players engrossed in a musically intimate conversation. This is not a performance appropriate for accompanying dancers but might instead be seen as an exploration of hidden possibilities of meaning in the music. In so doing it reveals some of its underlying mystery, including, perhaps, a darker side. Just as in an Ibsen play, where the surface bonhomie, jollity and social nicety can be hiding something more sinister, in Scandinavian dance music there are at times hints of a troublesome undercurrent below the surface. So the decision to open proceedings with �Fossgrimen,� a fiddle tune from Norway's Setesdal valley, is perhaps significant. A fossgrimen is a mythical creature, a kind of water-sprite living in waterfalls from whom fiddle-players were considered to have learned their skills and for that were not universally welcomed, with the fiddle considered to be the devil's instrument. Kr�ta by Ed�n/Kvifte/Nesheim trio Tellef Kvifte takes the lead melody on most tracks but on the Swedish �Polska from Per Myhr,� having played a repeated introductory riff on the sj�fl�yte, with Mats Ed�n providing an amorphous textural accompaniment below and Nesheim adding some quiet tinkling, it's Ed�n who introduces the tune on the fiddle with Kvifte proceeding to play in unison. It's a short track and almost as soon as it gets going things start to fragment and everything grind to a halt.

items.body: Düsseldorf and Electronic music have been inextricably linked for decades. The city has produced a distinctive musical legacy in which experimentation, electronics, minimalism, and a fascination with the future have always been central. It is a history that stretches back to the 1970s and 1980s, when electronic music, with Kraftwerk as its pioneering flagship, was not so much regarded as an exercise in nostalgia, but rather as a way of looking towards the future. It was within this tradition that Mängelexemplar emerged in 2011, simply abbreviated as MNGLXMPLR. The Düsseldorf duo, consisting of Lilli B. and Joa H., found their place in the international underground with a distinctive blend of Minimal-Wave and Electro-Pop. Their name — stripped of its vowels to become the almost cryptic MNGLXMPLR — seems perfectly suited to their musical universe: sleek, unconventional, and just a little elusive. Over the years, MNGLXMPLR have established themselves as a familiar name on the scene, performing at numerous festivals and venues both in Germany and abroad. With their new album, “Neue Zukunft,” released this spring on Infacted Recordings, they continue their exploration of Minimal-Wave, delivering an opus that feels darker, harder, and more intense. I spoke with both protagonists about the album, their musical journey, and the future of MNGLXMPLR. (Courtesy by Inferno Sound Diaries) Q: MNGLXMPLR has now been active for more than ten years. Looking back, what are the first thoughts that come to mind? What have been the defining moments or biggest highlights so far, and how would you say the band has evolved over the years? M:More than ten years… that’s quite a statement. The funny thing is, there was never a ten-year plan. We founded MNGLXMPLR because we wanted to make music. One year became five, five became ten – and suddenly here we are. There have been intense phases, quiet phases, great shows, frustrating moments, and countless ideas that never made it anywhere. That’s part of it. The biggest change is probably that we’ve become much more confident in our own musical language. In the beginning, there was more searching and experimenting. Today, we have a much better sense of what feels right for MNGLXMPLR. But we don’t want to turn that into a formula. The moment you know exactly what the next track is going to sound like, things become boring. There have been many highlights over the years – releases, concerts, travels and encounters that happened through the music. But the biggest highlight is actually very simple: we’re still here. And we’re still curious. Q: It took several years for “Neue Zukunft” to finally see the light of day. I imagine that period brought about changes – not only in terms of your studio setup, but also in your songwriting and creative process. Could you tell us a little about how you have evolved and how that development shaped the album? M:“Neue Zukunft” took its time. A lot changed at Carismastudios during those years. The studio evolved, new equipment was added, different projects emerged, and we experimented with different ways of working. Some of those experiments eventually became part of the album. There are tracks that existed for years before they found their final form. We kept coming back to them, changing things, removing things, and sometimes simply leaving them alone for a while. Our songwriting has become more intuitive over time. We don’t sit down and say, ‘Today we’re going to write a minimal track’. A song can start with a beat, a sound, a voice, or simply a certain mood. The emotional side has also become more important. We wanted the emotion to already be present in the music, rather than being added later through production. The result has become harder and more direct in some places, but the minimalist foundation has remained. And we have no problem with a few rough edges. For us, perfect doesn’t automatically mean interesting. Q: What can you tell us about “Neue Zukunft”? What is the central idea or concept behind the album, and how do you look back on the composition, recording and production process today? M:“Neue Zukunft” is about change and movement. It’s not a concept album in the classic sense. There isn’t one single story that you have to decode. It’s more like a collection of different moods and sides of MNGLXMPLR. Minimalist structures, darker atmospheres, harder sounds and emotional moments. We wanted to preserve these contrasts. The visual identity also became an important part of the album. For this, we are working with Düsseldorf fashion icon Ela Holscher, fashion designer Michaela Reinhardt-Beron and photographer Thomas Stelzmann. In Düsseldorf, music, fashion, photography and art have always been closely connected. So for us, this connection felt very natural. But we didn’t want to turn it into nostalgia. We have no interest in pretending it’s 1982 again. Düsseldorf has its history. We’re interested in what we can do with it today. This idea is also carried onto the stage. Sound, visuals, fashion and performance should become part of the same atmosphere. Q: The title “Neue Zukunft” immediately catches the eye – particularly at a time shaped by increasing geopolitical tensions, social uncertainty and war. At the same time, we are entering a new artistic era in which algorithms, AI and digital technologies are increasingly influencing how music is created and consumed. What does the title “Neue Zukunft” mean to you, and how does it reflect your view of the world today? M:We deliberately wanted a title that looks ahead. There is already enough dystopian language around us. Of course, we see what is happening in the world. War, political conflicts and uncertainty are part of the present. But “Neue Zukunft” is not about resignation. It’s about movement. The future is coming anyway. AI is obviously part of that future and is already changing the way music is created and consumed. We don’t use AI to create MNGLXMPLR. For us, the human process remains essential: writing, playing, recording, making mistakes and changing things. Electronic music, however, has always been closely connected to technological change. Synthesizers, samplers and computers changed the way musicians work. AI will be another major shift. We don’t think it makes sense to simply accept it blindly or reject it outright. You have to question it. You have to decide what you want to use from it and why. “Neue Zukunft” doesn’t mean that we know what tomorrow will look like. It means that we’re ready to find out. Q: These days, many listeners focus more on playlists and individual singles than on complete albums. I personally still believe that an album represents a comprehensive artistic statement. Do you think the album format remains relevant in an increasingly fragmented and fast-paced musical landscape? M:Absolutely. A single can work on its own. But an album gives it context. You can build an atmosphere, create tension and connect tracks that might work very differently as individual singles. That’s important to us. “Neue Zukunft” was made as an album, and the sequence of the tracks matters. And then there’s the album on vinyl. We like the physical experience. You take the record out of the sleeve, look at the artwork, put it on and listen. Then you turn it over. You can’t really speed that up. And maybe that’s exactly the point. In a world where everything is instantly available, a record forces you to slow down. You can even hold the music in your hands. Artwork, photography, design and music become one shared object. That still has value. Q: MNGLXMPLR is also very much a live band – you have even played in Belgium three times already. How important are live performances to your identity as a band? How do you transfer the atmosphere of your studio recordings to the stage, and what touring plans do you have in connection with “Neue Zukunft”? M:Playing live is extremely important to us. The studio is controlled; the stage isn’t. That’s exactly why we like it. We don’t want to simply reproduce “Neue Zukunft” live exactly as it sounds on the record. The live versions are more direct, more physical and sometimes even harder. But the atmosphere has to remain intact. The audience also changes the performance. You can prepare a set, but you can’t prepare a room. We’ve already played in Belgium three times, and every concert had its own character. That’s one of the reasons we enjoy playing abroad. With “Neue Zukunft”, we want to play a new series of concerts across Europe. Looking towards 2027, we also want to move beyond the classic minimal scene, discover other Electronic scenes and play larger stages. The visual side will also become more important. Not as decoration, but as part of the performance. Sound, light, fashion, photography and movement should belong together. We don’t want people to simply hear “Neue Zukunft”. We want them to experience it. Q: You come from Düsseldorf, a city that will forever be associated with KRAFTWERK. To what extent do you still feel this artistic legacy among Electronic artists from the city today? Has Düsseldorf’s musical heritage directly or indirectly influenced your own work? M:Kraftwerk is unavoidable. If you make Electronic music in Düsseldorf, you grow up with that history. But Düsseldorf is much more than Kraftwerk. DAF, Die Krupps and many other artists developed completely different forms of electronic music. What connects them for us isn’t necessarily a particular sound. It’s an attitude: experimenting, reducing, making music physical, questioning things, and not caring too much whether someone has already invented a genre for it. We can relate to that a lot. But we don’t want to sound like Kraftwerk, or DAF, or Die Krupps. They’ve already done that – and pretty well. So our connection to Düsseldorf’s musical history is more indirect. You grow up surrounded by music, art, fashion, photography and clubs. You absorb that environment without necessarily realizing it. And years later, you realize how much of it has stayed with you. So yes, Düsseldorf has influenced MNGLXMPLR. But we don’t want to become a heritage band. We respect the past, but musically, we live in the here and now. Look back. Take with you what matters. Keep moving forward.

items.body: Are we better off alone Will I come into my own Are we better off alone Being understood by someone is a comfort until the relationship ends and their imagined opinion starts conducting an inspection of everything wrong with you. Boy Harsher’s Faulty inhabits that uncomfortable interval between asking to be wanted and wondering what that wanting has cost. Jae Matthews sings as though the verdict may already be in, while Augustus Muller gives her doubts enough room to move. The question of being better off alone becomes something to turn over on the dancefloor, where thinking clearly has always been optional. The song accompanies the release of Get Mean, out now following its September 18 arrival through Atlantic Records. Their first album since 2022’s The Runner, the twelve-track record follows the end of Matthews and Muller’s romantic relationship in early 2024, after a period of family loss, personal upheaval, and creative uncertainty. Continuing the band meant finding a way to work together while the terms of their lives were changing. That makes the tenderness of Faulty particularly affecting: the people making this music understand how complicated its questions can become. A kicking beat, busy hi-hats, and quivering synths set Faulty in motion. Its dark disco rhythm has some of Careful’s physical insistence, softened by broad synth pads and little descending electronic notes that drop through the arrangement with a rounded, almost playful boop. When the beat pauses to breathe, the synths take on a Vangelis-like warble, briefly opening the song into something more spacious and cinematic. The rhythm returns beneath a lead synth that bends up and down in pitch, while Matthews keeps her voice hushed and close, breathing the words with a tenderness that borders on resignation. The lyrics put affection and self-assessment in an uncomfortable room together. Asking whether she is faulty gives another person the power to diagnose her; asking whether she will come into her own begins to take some of that power back. Repetition keeps either possibility from becoming a settled conclusion. Matthews sounds caught between wanting to be held and recognizing how much of herself might be waiting outside the relationship. Directed by Boy Harsher and shot on 35mm with cinematography by Owen Smith-Clark, the final video in the Get Mean series returns to a room lined in brown wood paneling. A television glows blue on a black stand, a small fan sits by the window, and a microphone cable trails across the carpet. Against that ordinary setting, the changing cast look dressed for entirely different evenings: a white cowboy hat, metallic bodysuits, striped knitwear, black boots. Each person seems to have brought a private version of the same bad night. The camera moves from fixed views of the room into close-ups of faces, hands, and bodies moving past one another. People share the frame, lean together, or briefly touch, but proximity never quite settles the question in the chorus. There is a lovely awkwardness to it: the self-consciousness of dancing at home, followed by the sudden absorption of forgetting you are being watched. By the end, the people have gone and the television is still there. The room has held all that feeling without offering anyone an answer. Watch the video for Faulty below: Across Get Mean, the effort to keep going takes several musical forms. Writing began to move again when Matthews took to the road, travelling through West Texas, the Pacific Northwest, and South Florida. The album was eventually recorded in eight locations across the United States, Mexico, and Italy, its unsettled circumstances allowing new sounds and approaches into the duo’s work. Matthews describes it as “what I had to give during the most extreme period of my life.” The three singles we covered ahead of its release made clear how much that offering could contain. The first indication came with Jeans, released in June. Its springy guitar figure and bubbling electronics brought a new wave directness to Boy Harsher, with a steel-slide twang giving the song a western accent. Our earlier comparison to the Pretenders still fits the way Matthews’ cool delivery rides that guitar, while the buoyancy also suggests Muller’s work in Safe Mind. Beneath the cheek is a sharp little study of ambition: the dream of escaping a small town, the dream of becoming somebody, and the possibility of ending up selling an image of freedom by the pair. The band’s latex line-dancing video, conceived with Robert Palmer’s Addicted to Love in mind, makes that collision between aspiration, performance, and merchandise deliciously literal. Hard Beat, unveiled alongside July’s album announcement, tightens the pressure around a repeating bass-synth figure and an unrelenting kick. As we noted then, there is something of Depeche Mode’s Behind the Wheel in its meeting of motion, desire, and surrendered control. Matthews moves between confession and invitation while the rhythm keeps pushing ahead. Its video makes those exchanges physical through an elaborate leg brace, a Cadillac, and a handheld camcorder, drawing medical hardware, automotive controls, and the invasive act of filming into the same uneasy visual language. Within the album, the track preserves the severe club momentum that has long served Boy Harsher so well, giving the softer and more openly melodic songs something solid to push against. August’s Tough Luck (When You Don’t Call) puts a warmer arrangement around the indignity of waiting for someone to remember you exist. A brisk new wave beat, rounded bass, bright keyboards, and short bursts of distorted guitar carry Matthews’ unhappy drawl toward the sort of pop chorus that can make despair briefly feel sociable. Her insistence that she is okay sounds increasingly like something she needs to practice. Our earlier review followed that idea into the lyric video, where yellow karaoke lettering crosses the blue screen of a CRT television. Created with vintage video equipment by Sean McGuirk and shot by Jesse Korman, it turns failed communication into a singalong with nobody else visibly present. Heard beside Faulty, the song makes the eventual question of solitude feel earned. Coming Home opens with Matthews in a smoky, Lynchian register, her voice suspended over steadily repeating synths and a breezy dance beat. The low guitar tones bring New Order to mind, with the melodic weight of a Peter Hook bassline translated onto guitar. That combination gives the song an appealing pull between bodily ease and emotional uncertainty. The rhythm leaves the windows open; the vocal suggests someone still deciding whether it is safe to come inside. Here, the album’s broader musical interests allow vulnerability to sound inviting without making it seem simple. Ice Pick (Walk Away) makes a particularly satisfying turn toward gothic rock. The parenthetical invites a Sisters of Mercy comparison before the guitar has even had its say, and the melody strengthens the association with their First and Last and Always period. A deep post-punk bass groove and the crunchy splash of the drum machine give the track a familiar dry ice chill. Matthews’ tender delivery moderates that severity, placing a vulnerable voice inside an arrangement with its collar firmly turned up. The resemblance is a pleasure to hear, especially from a duo whose love of this music has often been expressed through a different set of instruments. Pray 4 Me lets the bass loosen its hips. Soft synth pads, a sexy funk groove, and quivering bell tones bring a strain of Bryan Ferry-eque sophisti-pop into the album, expanding its capacity for pleasure as well as distress. There is a suppleness to the arrangement that makes this feel like a natural extension of the record’s emotional dynamic range. Desire, after all, does not become less complicated when somebody gives it a particularly good bassline. Boy Harsher sounds comfortable letting elegance and appetite share the same song. The album closes with Bleed, setting trip-hop beats against crystalline synths and low, bone-marrow-churning bass. Imagine the Bristol-born genre taking shape inside the electric dreams of the mid-1980s: the drums with a twitching hi-hat and thump have that low, unhurried weight, while the electronics give the space around them a cool, glassy clarity. After the movement of the preceding songs, this slower finish lets the record exhale. Its change of pace offers a place to sit with everything that has happened. Get Mean gives Matthews and Muller’s affection for post-punk, synthpop, goth, and dance music considerably more room to misbehave. They have grown as people, their lives have changed, and their music has had the good sense to evolve. Those expecting Pain on an endless loop, or Careful with a fresh set of track titles, may find this development inconvenient. For listeners who share Jae and Gus’s musical curiosity, there is pleasure in hearing them loosen up, follow their enthusiasms, and discover what this new chapter of their partnership can become. And if Get Mean isn’t the Boy Harsher you ordered, well, tough shit. Listen to Get Mean below and order the album here. Additional listening and purchase options are available here. GET MEAN by Boy Harsher Since forming in 2014, Matthews and Muller have taken Boy Harsher from the small cassette run of Lesser Man, whose Pain spread widely online, through Yr Body Is Nothing in 2016, the Country Girl EP in 2017, and Careful in 2019. Their background in film became central to 2022’s The Runner, which they wrote, produced, directed, and scored. Their work in cinema also includes The Lonely Woman, their debut feature as directors, starring Chloë Sevigny, FKA twigs, and Sturgill Simpson. Boy Harsher’s The Heartbreak Tour resumes September 25 at Basilica Hudson, with North American dates running through November 5 at New York’s Knockdown Center. items._cn_summary: Boy Harsher新专辑《Get Mean》围绕二人组合情感关系破裂后的创作展开，十二首曲目延续其暗潮与合成器驱动的后朋克路线。歌曲《Faulty》以强kick鼓底、密集hi-hat与颤动合成器构建暗黑迪斯科律动，合成器垫音宽厚柔软，偶尔穿插类似Vangelis风格的空旷合成器颤音，在紧凑节奏中开辟出电影感的空间。歌词围绕自我审视与渴望被理解的张力展开，反复提问的结构让结论悬而未决。Matthews以低语般的人声传递脆弱与决绝并存的情感，Muller的编曲则给予这些疑问足够的呼吸空间。35mm胶片MV延续系列视觉语言，木质墙板房间与蓝色电视光构成普通室内空间，着装各异的舞者在此短暂交汇又彼此疏离，身体的接近始终无法回答歌曲提出的核心问题。专辑由Atlantic Records发行，是二人自2022年《The Runner》以来的首张全长作品。

items.body: ケイシー・カンジェローシ 初来日リサイタルに寄せて 世界中のパーカッショニストを魅了する演奏家・作曲家、ケイシー・カンジェローシ。その初来日リサイタルが、2026年9月26日（土）、長久手市文化の家 森のホール（愛知県）で開催される。公演に寄せられた3人のコメントと映像から、その魅力を紹介する。 打楽器音楽の常識を覆す発想 新野将之（マルチパーカッショニスト） 僕が最も敬愛する打楽器奏者、ケイシー・カンジェローシ。 彼の音楽には、「打楽器でここまでできるのか！」という驚きが詰まっています。卓越したテクニックはもちろん、タンバリンやスネアドラムの可能性を極限まで追求し、石を打ち合わせる音、電子音、パントマイムまで音楽の中へ大胆に取り込んでしまう。その発想は、まさに打楽器音楽の常識を覆すものです。 そして何より面白いのは、彼の音楽が「聴く」だけでは終わらないこと。音、身体、動き、空間……すべてをひとつの表現として融合させ、クラシック音楽の枠を飛び越え、新しいエンターテイメントへと昇華させていきます。 アートでありながら、圧倒的に楽しい。 知的でありながら、魂を揺さぶる。 打楽器の未来を切り拓いてきた開拓者、ケイシー・カンジェローシ。その唯一無二の世界を、ぜひ生で体感してください！ ﻿ 身体表現と、超絶技巧の打楽器演奏を一体化 小室敬幸（音楽ライター） 1982年にアメリカで生まれたケイシー・カンジェローシは、打楽器を音だけでなく、奏者の身体や身振りまで含む舞台表現として捉えているユニークな打楽器奏者で作曲家だ。今回のリサイタルで演奏されるティエリー・ドゥ・メイ《Silence Must Be!》は、その志向を象徴する選曲である。メイはローザスを率いるアンヌ・テレサ・ドゥ・ケースマイケルら、ベルギーのコンテンポラリーダンスと密接に活動し、音楽的にはルイ・アンドリーセンらに連なるヨーロッパ的なミニマリズムを結びつけた作曲家。そのメイのような音楽の系譜に位置づけられるカンジェローシは、代表作《Meditation No.1》を含む自身の作品でも、打つ、振る、構えるといった動作や反復が、音と同じほど重要な表現になる。ダンスや演劇に通じる身体表現と、超絶技巧の打楽器演奏を一体化させており、今や世界中の若いパーカショニストを魅了している作曲家なのだ。目で見て真価が味わえる音楽なので、日本で初めて行う本格的リサイタルは必聴・必見である！ フィクションとフィジカルのあわい 加藤綾子（ヴァイオリニスト） YouTubeやInstagram上で切り抜かれる、カンジェローシの身体。バストアップであったり、手元や指先であったりするそれらを画面越しに見たとき、わたしたちは、まずそのディテールに心を奪われる。その身体は多彩な楽器を、ごく当たり前に扱う（ように見える）。ティエリー・ドゥ・メイのスコアを、美しく実現する。石ころもオルゴールも、スティックも、あまりに自然に振る舞うものだから、まるでオブジェクト・シアターを鑑賞しているような感覚に陥る。 そのうえで、彼は切実な演奏者であり続ける。鍛錬された身振りは、どこまでいっても彼自身あるいは他者の音楽を実践し、批評するためにある。その切実さが、きっと、ひとびとの全身を鷲掴む。画面越しではない、実存として長久手に立つ「カンジェローシ」は、音楽というフィクションとフィジカルのあわいを鮮やかに描き、突きつけてくれるだろう。──つまり、生で見るカンジェローシの演奏は、めっちゃすごくてやばいはず、ということです。 公演情報 ケイシー・カンジェローシ パーカッションリサイタル TENDRILS 2026年9月26日（土）16:00 長久手市文化の家 森のホール（愛知県） 公演詳細：https://bunkanoie.jp/archives/9250

items._cn_summary: 本文围绕打击乐演奏家、作曲家凯西·坎杰罗西即将在日本爱知县长久手市举办的首场独奏会，汇集了三位不同身份评论者的视角。文章指出坎杰罗西将打击乐从单纯的音色范畴拓展为融合身体动作、舞台空间与戏剧性表达的综合性艺术形式，其音乐中纳入了电子音、肢体哑剧甚至石块碰撞等非常规声源。评论特别提及比利时作曲家蒂埃里·德·梅的作品《Silence Must Be!》，该作品源于欧洲极简主义与当代舞蹈的传统，与坎杰罗西自身作品中对打击动作与声音并置的处理方式一脉相承。文章强调坎杰罗西的演出需要亲临现场方能完整感受其在视觉与听觉层面所构建的独特张力。

items.body:
特集『ジョン・コルトレーン生誕100年』
ALL ABOUT JAZZ
NO. 341
#11 Lewis Porter『John Coltrane His Life and Music』
ルイス・ポーター『コルトレーン　人と音楽』
2026年9月19日
ゲスト・ コントリビューター

text: Gene Lees ジーン・リース

Univ of Michigan Press
1998

ジョン・コルトレーンが41歳を目前にしてこの世を去ってから31年が経つが、彼は依然として謎に満ちた存在であり続けている。それは私にとってだけでなく、これまで書物の中で彼の人物像を捉えようと試みてきた数多くの人々にとっても同様だ。ルイス・ポーターの『John Coltrane: His Life and Music』が出版されたことで、彼に関する英語の著作は計8冊を数えることになったが、ポーターの著書を含め、そのいずれもが彼の人間性について深い洞察を与えてくれるものではない。

気軽に読める本をお探しなら、この本はやめておいたほうがいいだろう。私生活に関する記述は比較的少なく、その一部も推測に基づいたものだ。

本書は徹底して音楽そのものに焦点を当てている。それゆえ、和声（ハーモニー）について十分な理解があり、楽譜を読みこなす能力を備えたミュージシャンでない限り、本書を手に取ることはお勧めできない。しかし、もしあなたがミュージシャン、とりわけジャズ・ミュージシャンであるなら、急いで書店へ走り、本書を買い求めるべきだ。そして、数日や数週間ではなく、数ヶ月をかけてじっくりと研究する覚悟を決めてほしい。本書は、ジャズ・ミュージシャンの芸術を扱った音楽分析として、私がこれまでに読んだ中で最高傑作と言えるものだ。その内容は実に見事である。ポーター博士は誠実な研究者であると同時に、ラトガース大学の音楽准教授であり、自身もジャズ・ミュージシャンである。彼はピアニストだが、かつては15年にわたりサックス奏者として活動していた。偉大なサックス奏者――ある見方によれば同世代で最高の奏者――の業績を論じるその言葉の端々に、彼自身のそうした経験が如実に表れている。

自分はといえば、コルトレーンをよく知っていたとは言えない。そもそも、彼を「よく知る」ことなど可能だったのかどうかも定かではないからだ。確かに私たちは親しい間柄にあり、私が『ダウンビート』誌の編集長を務めていた頃には、彼がシカゴの自宅へ夕食に来てくれることも時折あった。彼に対する私の印象は、ポーターがインタビューした他の人々が抱いているものと同じだ。穏やかで、言葉を発するときは明晰だが、普段はとても物静か、そして驚くほど謙虚な人だった。凡庸な音楽的才能の持ち主ほど、往々にして肥大した自尊心を持っているものだが、私にはそれがいつも不思議でならなかった。一方、傑出した才能を持つ人々は、控えめな態度をとる傾向がある。おそらく彼らは常に自身の能力の限界を押し広げようとしており、その芸術そのものが彼らを謙虚にさせるのだろう。ジョンはまさにそのような人物だった。ポーターの著書でも何度か引用されているが、彼は音楽的にも哲学的にも、自分が探し求めているものをまだ完全には見つけ出せていないと語っていた。彼と一緒にバルトークの『弦楽器、打楽器とチェレスタのための音楽』を聴いたときのことを覚えている。彼はストラヴィンスキーの音楽には（多くのジャズ・ミュージシャンがそうであるように）精通していたが、その曲はそれまで聴いたことがなかったようだった。彼はその曲に完全に聴き入っていた。その間、当時３歳くらいだった私の息子が彼の膝によじ登り、くつろいでいたのだ。私の中の彼の姿は、まさにそんなふうに、小さな子供に対して心を開き、優しく接する姿として記憶されている。率直に言って、私はジョンという人間が大好きだった。

彼がかつてヘロイン中毒だったことは広く知られている。彼は自力で、しかも早い段階でその依存を断ち切ったが、後年になってLSDを使用するようになった（このことは私自身知らなかったのだが）。おそらくそれは、彼が音楽を通じて追い求めていた神秘体験を求めてのことだったのだろう。ジョンの音楽は本質的に宗教的な探求であり、ポーターが記しているように、彼は世界のあらゆる宗教に魅了されていた。同様に、彼は出会うあらゆる種類の音楽にも関心を寄せていた。彼は子供の一人に「ラヴィ」と名付けたが、これは友人の一人であり、偉大なシタール奏者であるラヴィ・シャンカールにちなんだものだった（ちなみにラヴィという名の人物は、傑出した前衛サックス奏者でもあったが、その才能は十分に評価されていなかった）。

コルトレーンは1950年代後半、ジャズ界の主要な人物として頭角を現した。ノースカロライナ州に生まれた彼は、フィラデルフィアで、生涯の友人であり同じく重要なサックス奏者であるベニー・ゴルソンと共に、音楽家としての才能を磨いていった。彼がその才能を開花させ、人々の注目を集めるきっかけとなったのは、マイルス・デイヴィス・グループへの参加だった。

ジョンは硬質なトーンで演奏すると言われており、その演奏を「怒りに満ちている」と評する向きもあった。彼はそのことを不思議に思っていた。彼は私にこう言ったものだ。「なぜみんな、僕の演奏が怒っているなんて言うんだろう？ 何に対しても怒ってなんかないのに」。ポーター博士の著書によれば、彼はこの点を気にかけ、他の人々にも同じようなことを口にしていたそうだ。私には、ジョンの音色は並外れて美しいものに聞こえた。私は彼がバラードばかりを演奏したレコーディング・セッションに立ち会ったことがある――実際、彼が私にライナーノーツの執筆を依頼したためにそこにいたのだが、私はその通りに執筆した。そのセッションでの、心を奪われるほどに柔らかな演奏のことは今でも忘れられない（その印象はアルバムにも記録されている）。それは生涯、私の心に残り続けるだろ。彼は亡くなったシンガーのジョニー・ハートマンともアルバムを制作しているが、そこでも彼のそうした側面がはっきりと表れている。

しかし、彼は驚くべき情熱を込めて演奏することができた。少なくともキャリアの初期において、彼はアルペジオ（分散和音）を多用する奏法に強い関心を抱いていた。次々と和音を積み重ねていくかのような（サックスという楽器の構造上、物理的には不可能なことではあるが）その猛烈な速さの演奏は、評論家のアイラ・ギトラーによって「シーツ・オブ・サウンド（音の奔流）」と形容され、その呼び名はその後も定着することとなった。また、彼のソロは非常に長く、15分以上に及ぶことも珍しくなかった。1963年のニューポート・ジャズ・フェスティバルで録音された『マイ・ファヴァリット・シングス』は、17分24秒にも及ぶ。こうした演奏の長さはマイルス・デイヴィスを苛立たせ、ある有名なやり取りを生むことにもなった。彼がマイルスに「ソロに入ると、どうやって抜け出せばいいのか分からなくなることがある」と打ち明けた際、マイルスは「口からホーンを外してみたらどうだ」と答えたと伝えられている。

ジョンの宗教的な探求は、最期まで続いた。彼はジャズ特有の安定したビートを避け、より自由なアプローチをとるようになり、その結果、聴衆の一部を――さらには共演するミュージシャンの一部さえも――失うことになった。偉大かつ多大な影響力を持つピアニストのマッコイ・タイナーが1965年末に去り、続いて長年ドラマーを務めた名手エルヴィン・ジョーンズも1966年に脱退したが、二人はインタビューで揃ってこのバンドを「ただの騒音」と評している。

コルトレーンが登場した当時、ジャズ界には傑出した、極めて個性的なミュージシャンが数多く存在していました。今日、これほどの豊かさと比較できるものはなく、若手の有力な演奏家の多くは、過去の遺産を掘り起こすような、いわゆる「レトロ・ジャズ」を演奏している。もはや、なすべきことは何も残されていないのかもしれない。アルノルト・シェーンベルクが調性中心を回避した音楽を書き始めてから、すでに１世紀近くが経過した。ミュージシャンたちはそこに興味を抱くかもしれないが、一般大衆は一貫して無関心なままである。どうやら、調性から離れていくミュージシャンに大衆の耳がついていける範囲には、自ずと限界があるようだ。

あらゆる種類の「シリアス・ミュージック」が危機に瀕している。米国のクラシック音楽ラジオ局は、ロックを聴いて育ち、それ以外の音楽を知らない人々の神経をなだめるための、一種の「高級なBGM」を流す局へと変貌しつつある。北米においてジャズを放送するラジオ局は減少の一途をたどっている。ロサンゼルスには現在、そうした局が一つもないが、1940年代半ばには同市内に40もの局が存在していた。大手出版社はジャズや、あるいは往年のポピュラー・ソングにさえ関心を示していない。そうした状況を補っているのが、イェール大学をはじめとする大学の出版局だ。昨秋、音楽関連の書籍を対象としたASCAP（米国作曲家作詞家出版者協会）のディームズ・テイラー賞が授与された際、全10賞のうち8つが大学出版局の刊行物に贈られた。ポーター博士の著書も、ミシガン大学出版局から刊行されたものである。

そして、ポーター博士の著書は、彼をそのような存在たらしめた要因を実に見事に分析した一冊だ。あらゆる音楽学校に備えておくべき本であり、すべてのジャズ・ミュージシャンが読むべき――いや、研究すべき――一冊であることは間違いない。

*初出

1928~2010。バークリー音大卒。ジャズ評論家、作詞家、歌手、音楽史家。1959~1961「ダウンビート」誌編集長。「Quiet Nights of Quiet Stars」の英詩家として知られる。ヴォーカリストとして『Gebe Lees sings Gene Lees』など４枚のアルバムを制作。
